section.title: The Ark, the Table, and the Lampstand
section.sectionRationale: On the mountain, God moves from law to dwelling: He asks for a willing offering from the people and gives Moses the pattern for the three central furnishings of the Holy Place and Most Holy Place, the ark where He will meet with Israel, the table of the Bread of the Presence, and the golden lampstand.
section.thesis: God tells Moses to have Israel bring a freewill offering so that He may dwell among them, and gives the exact pattern for the ark and mercy seat where He will meet with Moses, the table for the Bread of the Presence, and the golden lampstand.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the call for a willing offering so God may dwell among His people; the ark and mercy seat where God will meet with Moses; the table and the Bread of the Presence; and the golden lampstand.

units.label: An offering so God may dwell among them
units.note: a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them

media.alt: Gold, silver, and colored yarn gathered before a tent
media.caption: God asks for a willing offering so that He may make His dwelling among His people.

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,
“Tell the Israelites to bring Me an offering. You are to receive My offering from every man whose heart compels him.
This is the offering you are to accept from them: gold, silver, and bronze;
blue, purple, and scarlet yarn; fine linen and goat hair;
ram skins dyed red and fine leather; acacia wood;
olive oil for the light; spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense;
and onyx stones and gemstones to be mounted on the ephod and breastpiece.
And they are to make a {{sanctuary|sanctuary}} for Me, so that I may dwell among them.
You must make the tabernacle and design all its furnishings according to the {{pattern|pattern}} I show you.

units.label: The ark and the mercy seat
units.note: there I will meet with you

verses.text: And they are to construct an ark of acacia wood, two and a half cubits long, a cubit and a half wide, and a cubit and a half high.
Overlay it with pure gold both inside and out, and make a gold molding around it.
Cast four gold rings for it and fasten them to its four feet, two rings on one side and two on the other.
And make poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold.
Insert the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark, in order to carry it.
The poles are to remain in the rings of the ark; they must not be removed.
And place inside the ark the {{testimony|Testimony}}, which I will give you.
And you are to construct a {{mercyseat|mercy seat}} of pure gold, two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide.
Make two cherubim of hammered gold at the ends of the mercy seat,
one cherub on one end and one on the other, all made from one piece of gold.
And the cherubim are to have wings that spread upward, overshadowing the mercy seat. The cherubim are to face each other, looking toward the mercy seat.
Set the mercy seat atop the ark, and put the Testimony that I will give you into the ark.
And I will meet with you there above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim that are over the ark of the Testimony; I will speak with you about all that I command you regarding the Israelites.

units.label: The table and the Bread of the Presence

verses.text: You are also to make a table of acacia wood two cubits long, a cubit wide, and a cubit and a half high.
Overlay it with pure gold and make a gold molding around it.
And make a rim around it a handbreadth wide and put a gold molding on the rim.
Make four gold rings for the table and fasten them to the four corners at its four legs.
The rings are to be close to the rim, to serve as holders for the poles used to carry the table.
Make the poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold, so that the table may be carried with them.
You are also to make the plates and dishes, as well as the pitchers and bowls for pouring drink offerings. Make them out of pure gold.
And place the {{bread|Bread of the Presence}} on the table before Me at all times.

units.label: The golden lampstand
units.note: according to the pattern shown you on the mountain

verses.text: Then you are to make a lampstand of pure, hammered gold. It shall be made of one piece, including its base and shaft, its cups, and its buds and petals.
Six branches are to extend from the sides of the lampstand, three on one side and three on the other.
There are to be three cups shaped like almond blossoms on the first branch, each with buds and petals, three on the next branch, and the same for all six branches that extend from the lampstand.
And on the lampstand there shall be four cups shaped like almond blossoms with buds and petals.
For the six branches that extend from the lampstand, a bud must be under the first pair of branches, a bud under the second pair, and a bud under the third pair.
The buds and branches are to be all of one piece with the lampstand, hammered out of pure gold.
Make seven lamps and set them up on the lampstand so that they illuminate the area in front of it.
The wick trimmers and their trays must be of pure gold.
The lampstand and all these utensils shall be made from a talent of pure gold.
See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.

sanctuary.gloss: A holy place, a sanctuary. Its purpose is stated plainly in verse 8: so that I may dwell among them, showing that the tabernacle exists for the sake of God's presence with His people, not merely as a ritual center.

pattern.gloss: A pattern, model, or blueprint. Moses is shown a heavenly original which the earthly tabernacle only copies, a detail Hebrews later develops to show that the earthly sanctuary was always a shadow pointing to a greater, heavenly reality.

testimony.gloss: The Testimony, referring to the stone tablets of the covenant law. Placed inside the ark, it is the witness of the covenant terms Israel had agreed to, kept literally beneath the place where God's presence would rest.

mercyseat.gloss: Mercy seat, atonement cover. Related to the verb for making atonement, this gold lid covering the ark is where the blood of atonement would be sprinkled on the Day of Atonement and where God's presence met Israel above the very place the law was kept.

bread.gloss: Bread of the Presence, or bread of the face, kept continually on the table before the LORD. It symbolized Israel's ongoing fellowship with, and dependence on, God, offered to Him and later eaten by the priests.

basic.context: On the mountain, God shifts from giving law to describing a dwelling place. He asks Israel for a willing offering of valuable materials, then gives Moses exact instructions for the ark, where He will meet with Moses above the mercy seat, the table holding bread always kept before Him, and a golden lampstand.
basic.hermeneutics: These are historical instructions for building Israel's actual sanctuary, not a symbolic code to be decoded item by item. The furnishings served real, concrete purposes, housing the covenant tablets, providing bread and light, while their placement and materials also carried theological weight about God's holiness and presence.
basic.originalLanguages: God asks for a mikdash, sanctuary, built according to a heavenly tavnit, pattern, so that He may dwell among His people. Inside the ark rests the edut, the Testimony of the covenant, beneath the kapporet, the mercy seat, where God says He will meet with Moses.
basic.typology: The ark and mercy seat, where God meets His people above the covenant law and where atonement blood would later be sprinkled, foreshadow Christ, in whom mercy and the demands of the law meet perfectly. The lampstand's continual light points to Christ as the light of the world, and the Bread of the Presence anticipates the Bread of Life.
basic.christ: Paul calls Jesus the hilasterion, the same word used for the mercy seat, in Romans 3:25, the place where God's justice and mercy meet in a sacrifice. Christ is the true meeting place between God and His people, the true bread that sustains life, John 6:35, and the true light, John 8:12.
basic.god: God's desire is explicit: 'that I may dwell among them.' The sheer costliness and beauty of gold, fine linen, and skilled craftsmanship shows how much God's presence is worth, while the exact pattern shown to Moses shows His holiness allows no human improvisation in how He is approached.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 3:25 calls Christ the mercy seat, the place of propitiation. Hebrews 9:1-5 describes these very furnishings as a copy of heavenly things. John 6:35 and John 8:12 present Jesus as the true bread and the true light these objects foreshadowed.
basic.oneStory: God asks His redeemed people for a willing offering so He can dwell among them, giving exact patterns for the ark, table, and lampstand that will hold His presence, His provision, and His light. Every one of these furnishings finds its truest fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the meeting place, bread, and light for all who trust Him.

context.literary:
Exodus 25 opens the largest single block of instruction in the book. Chapters 25 to 31 describe the tabernacle; chapters 35 to 40 describe it being built, often in nearly the same words. Between the two blocks stands the golden calf, chapters 32 to 34. The design is deliberate. The plan for God's dwelling is given, the people break the covenant, God renews it, and then the dwelling is built exactly as planned. Few things in Exodus are repeated at such length, which tells the reader how much weight the author places on this material.

The instructions begin at the centre and move outward. The ark comes first, then the table and the lampstand, then the tent that covers them in chapter 26, and then the altar and courtyard in chapter 27. This is the order of holiness, not the order of construction. God describes His dwelling from the point where He meets with Moses, verse 22, out to the edge where ordinary Israelites will stand.

Within chapter 25 the structure is clear. Verses 1 to 9 state the purpose and the source of materials. Three furnishings follow, each introduced with a command to make it and each described by its wood, its gold, its rings and its poles. The chapter is framed by the word 'pattern,' verses 9 and 40, which closes the unit with a warning to follow what was shown on the mountain.

The chapter also moves from Sinai toward the road. Every piece has rings and poles, verses 12 to 15, 26 to 28. Sinai's glory is being made portable. What was fixed on a mountain in chapter 24 will travel with Israel in a tent.
context.historical:
The materials listed in verses 3 to 7 were valuable, and a people just out of slavery might not be expected to have them. Exodus has already explained where they came from. God promised that Israel would not leave Egypt empty handed, Exodus 3:21-22, and the Egyptians gave them silver, gold and clothing, Exodus 12:35-36. The wealth of Egypt is now offered for the dwelling of the God who defeated Egypt's gods.

The offering was voluntary. When the call was repeated, Exodus 35:5, the response was so generous that Moses had to restrain the people from giving more, Exodus 36:5-7. A sanctuary built from a willing people's gifts was a mark of covenant love, not of forced tribute.

Acacia wood, used for every furnishing in this chapter, is a hard wood from trees that grow in the Sinai region and the dry country around it. Gold overlay on wood was a known technique for sacred objects in the ancient world.

The ark was a chest roughly the size the BSB footnote gives, about three and three quarter feet long. Chests carried on poles were used in the region for sacred objects, and winged guardian figures were familiar in the art of the ancient Near East, often flanking thrones. Israel's ark stands out not for its form but for what it lacks. There is no image of God upon it. The space above the mercy seat between the cherubim is empty, and from that empty space God speaks, verse 22. Inside the ark are the tablets of the covenant, the written words of the God who cannot be pictured.

The lampstand weighed a talent of gold, about seventy five pounds by the footnote's reckoning, verse 39. It stood in a room with no windows, so its light was the only light in the Holy Place.
context.canonical:
The ark goes on to play a central part in Israel's story. It leads the people through the Jordan, Joshua 3:3. At Shiloh it is called the ark of 'the LORD of Hosts, who sits enthroned between the cherubim,' 1 Samuel 4:4, and Israel's attempt to use it as a charm ends in its capture. Uzzah dies for touching it, 2 Samuel 6:6-7. Solomon places it beneath the great cherubim of the temple, 1 Kings 8:6-9, where the text notes there was nothing in it except the two stone tablets. The Psalms speak of God 'enthroned above the cherubim,' Psalm 99:1, and of the ark as His footstool, Psalm 132:7-8 and 1 Chronicles 28:2. Jeremiah foresees a day when the ark will no longer be missed, Jeremiah 3:16, because 'Jerusalem will be called The Throne of the LORD,' Jeremiah 3:17. The whole city will be what the ark once was.

The table and its bread are regulated in Leviticus 24:5-9: twelve loaves set out every Sabbath 'as a permanent covenant.' David and his men later eat this bread in need, 1 Samuel 21:6, and Jesus cites the incident, Matthew 12:3-4. Solomon multiplies the lampstands to ten, 1 Kings 7:49. Zechariah sees a golden lampstand fed by two olive trees, with the message 'Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit,' Zechariah 4:2-6.

The New Testament gathers all three furnishings. Hebrews lists the lampstand, the table, the bread and the ark with its cherubim and mercy seat, Hebrews 9:2-5, and quotes verse 40 to show that the tabernacle was 'a copy and shadow of what is in heaven,' Hebrews 8:5. Jesus calls Himself the bread of life and the light of the world, John 6:35 and 8:12. Revelation shows seven golden lampstands for the churches, Revelation 1:20, and the ark itself appearing in God's heavenly temple, Revelation 11:19.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wants Israel to understand that the whole purpose of the law and the covenant is presence. Verse 8 is the thesis of the chapter and arguably of the second half of Exodus: 'they are to make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them.' The Exodus did not end at the Red Sea or even at Sinai. It ends when God lives among His people, Exodus 29:45-46 and 40:34.

He also wants them to know that this presence is on God's terms. The repeated 'according to the pattern I show you,' verses 9 and 40, rules out improvisation. Israel had lived among the images and temples of Egypt; this sanctuary is to be shaped by revelation, not by imitation.

The order of the chapter teaches what matters most. God begins with the ark, the place where He will meet and speak, verse 22, and the tablets inside it. At the heart of Israel's worship is not an image but the covenant word, covered by the mercy seat. The table teaches that the twelve tribes live continually before God's face, and the lampstand that His house is never left in darkness.

Finally, Moses wants Israel to see that worship is a response of willing hearts. The first thing God asks for is an offering from 'every man whose heart compels him,' verse 2.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is prescriptive for Israel: it commands the construction of real objects. It is not prescriptive for the church in the same way. Christians are not told to build an ark, a table or a lampstand, and Hebrews explains why: these were 'a copy and shadow,' Hebrews 8:5, and Christ ministers in 'the sanctuary and true tabernacle,' Hebrews 8:2.

Yet principles carry forward. Giving for God's work is still to be willing rather than forced. Paul says the gift is acceptable when 'the eagerness is there,' 2 Corinthians 8:12, and that 'God loves a cheerful giver,' 2 Corinthians 9:7, which is the spirit of verse 2.

The insistence on the pattern also carries forward, though not as a building code. It teaches that God determines how He is to be approached. The New Testament fulfils that principle not with blueprints but with a Person: no one comes to the Father except through Christ, John 14:6.

Readers should also resist turning the furnishings into allegories unsupported by Scripture. The number of cups on the lampstand or the height of the table carry no stated meaning, and the chapter should not be made to say more than it says.

debates.question: How much theological meaning should be drawn from individual tabernacle details, such as the exact dimensions or the almond blossom shapes on the lampstand?

views.label: Restrained, big picture reading
views.case: Many interpreters caution against assigning allegorical meaning to every dimension or ornament, since Scripture does not explain most of them. The weight falls on God's stated purpose, dwelling among His people, verse 8. Hebrews itself declines to go into detail: 'we cannot discuss these things in detail now,' Hebrews 9:5.

views.label: Reading with canonical hints
views.case: Others note that Scripture itself draws out some details. The mercy seat is tied to atonement in Leviticus 16:14-15, and the Greek word for it is applied to Christ in Romans 3:25. The almond may carry meaning because the almond branch in Jeremiah 1:11-12 is linked to God watching over His word, and Aaron's staff produced almonds, Numbers 17:8.

debates.bearing: Both approaches agree on the main line: God's presence, provision and light are pictured here and fulfilled in Christ. The wise path is to press details only where other Scripture presses them.

debates.question: What exactly was the kapporet, and is 'mercy seat' the right name for it?

views.label: The place of atonement
views.case: The word shares its root with the verb kipper, 'to make atonement.' On the Day of Atonement the high priest sprinkled blood 'on the east side of the mercy seat,' Leviticus 16:14. The Greek translators rendered it with a word connected to propitiation, and the BSB footnote offers 'atonement cover.' On this view the object is named for what happened there.

views.label: A lid or cover, named for its function on the ark
views.case: Others argue that the root can simply mean 'to cover,' and that the word first described the gold lid that closed the ark. Its role in atonement came later, in Leviticus 16. The English 'mercy seat,' which goes back to William Tyndale, reflects theology more than etymology.

debates.bearing: The object was both. It covered the ark and the tablets, and it was the one place on earth where atoning blood was applied before God's presence. That double sense, covering and atonement, is exactly what makes it a fitting picture for the work of Christ.

study.originalLanguages:
The 'offering' of verse 2 is terumah, from the root rum, 'to be high' or 'to lift.' It describes something lifted off from a larger whole and set apart. The same word is used for portions set aside from sacrifices for the priests. Here Israel lifts a portion of the wealth God gave them out of Egypt and sets it apart for Him.

The phrase 'whose heart compels him' uses the verb nadav, 'to be willing' or 'to give freely.' From the same root comes nedavah, the 'freewill offering,' which is exactly what the people bring in Exodus 35:29 and keep bringing 'morning after morning' in Exodus 36:3. The Hebrew makes generosity a matter of the heart's own movement.

Verses 8 and 9 put two words side by side. God says 'that I may dwell,' using shakan, and names the structure mishkan, 'tabernacle' or 'dwelling place,' from the same root. Notice what God says He will dwell in: not 'in it' but 'among them.' The building serves a relationship with a people.

The 'ark' of verse 10 is aron, the ordinary word for a chest or box. It is the word used for Joseph's coffin in Genesis 50:26. It is not the word used for Noah's ark, Genesis 6:14, or for the basket of the infant Moses, Exodus 2:3; both of those are tevah. English uses 'ark' for both, but Hebrew keeps them apart.

The cherubim, keruvim, first appear guarding the way to the tree of life, Genesis 3:24. Elsewhere God is said to ride on a cherub, Psalm 18:10, and to be enthroned between them, 2 Samuel 6:2. Both the cherubim of the mercy seat and the lampstand are miqshah, 'hammered work,' verses 18 and 31, beaten out of one piece of gold rather than cast and joined.

The 'Bread of the Presence' in verse 30 is lechem panim, literally 'bread of the face.' The loaves lie 'before Me,' before God's face, at all times. The same word, panim, lies behind the priestly blessing, 'may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you,' Numbers 6:25. Hebrews 9:2 calls the same loaves 'the consecrated bread.'

The lampstand is menorah, and its cups are shaped like shaqed, the almond. The almond tree blossoms early, and Jeremiah records a wordplay on its name: he sees a shaqed branch, and God says He is shoqed, 'watching,' over His word, Jeremiah 1:11-12. Aaron's staff later sprouts almonds as a sign of God's choice, Numbers 17:8.

Finally, the kapporet of verse 17 was rendered by the Greek translators hilasterion. Hebrews 9:5 uses that word for the mercy seat, and Romans 3:25 uses the same word of Christ, where the BSB translates it 'atoning sacrifice.'

typology.type: The mercy seat between the cherubim, Exodus 25:17-22
typology.fulfillment: The mercy seat covered the tablets of the law, and once a year atoning blood was sprinkled on it, Leviticus 16:14-15, so that a holy God could meet with a sinful people above His own broken law. Paul uses the Greek name for this object when he says God 'presented Him as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood,' Romans 3:25. The escalation is striking: the mercy seat was hidden behind a veil, but Christ is publicly 'presented.' The type falls short in that the mercy seat needed fresh blood every year, while Christ offered Himself once for all, Hebrews 9:12.

typology.type: The Bread of the Presence on the table, Exodus 25:30
typology.fulfillment: Twelve loaves lay before God's face continually, one for each tribe, and were eaten by the priests in a holy place, Leviticus 24:5-9. They pictured Israel living before God and sustained at His table. Jesus declares, 'I am the living bread that came down from heaven,' John 6:51, and offers Himself not just to priests but to anyone who comes. The type falls short because the loaves were replaced every Sabbath and fed only a few; the bread Christ gives is 'for the life of the world,' and whoever eats it 'will live forever.'

The lampstand was the only light in the windowless Holy Place, shaped like a flowering almond tree, keeping God's house bright through the night. Jesus says, 'I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness,' John 8:12. Revelation shows the risen Christ standing 'among the lampstands,' which are His churches, Revelation 1:12-13 and 1:20, so the light now shines through His people, Matthew 5:14. The type points further still: the city of God needs no lamp, 'the Lamb is its lamp,' Revelation 21:23.

typology.type: The ark carrying the covenant tablets on the journey, Exodus 25:14-16
typology.fulfillment: The ark held the words of the covenant and was carried at the head of the people, Numbers 10:35, the place where God's throne met His law. Christ is the Word made flesh who 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and in Him God's law is perfectly kept and embodied. The new covenant writes that law on hearts, Jeremiah 31:33, rather than keeping it in a box. Jeremiah 3:16 foresaw that the ark would not be missed, and the fulfilment is that God's presence, once confined to one chest, now fills His people, 1 Corinthians 3:16.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the purpose statement of verse 8, 'that I may dwell among them.' John opens his Gospel by saying that the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, using a Greek verb built on the word for tent. What the tabernacle did in cloth and gold, Jesus does in flesh. And John adds, 'We have seen His glory,' the glory that would fill this tabernacle, Exodus 40:34.

It leads to Christ through the mercy seat. The place where God said 'I will meet with you there,' verse 22, was the lid over the covenant law, later sprinkled with atoning blood. Paul applies the Greek word for this object to Jesus: God 'presented Him as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood,' Romans 3:25. The meeting place between God and sinners is no longer a golden cover in a hidden room but a crucified and risen Person. The purpose Paul gives is also striking: the mercy seat showed God's forbearance, but Christ demonstrates His righteousness, Romans 3:25-26. Mercy and justice meet in Him.

It leads to Christ through the table. The Bread of the Presence lay before God continually. Jesus claims, 'I am the bread of life,' John 6:35, and contrasts Himself with the manna: 'Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, yet they died,' John 6:49. He also appeals to David eating this very bread to show that He, who is greater than the temple, is Lord of the Sabbath, Matthew 12:3-8.

It leads to Christ through the lampstand. In the temple courts, in the season of the Feast of Tabernacles, a festival recalling Israel's wilderness dwellings, John 7:2 and 8:20, Jesus said, 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12. John's Gospel had already said, 'In Him was life, and that life was the light of men,' John 1:4.

And it leads to Christ through the pattern. God showed Moses a pattern on the mountain, and Hebrews says that the earthly sanctuary was 'a copy and shadow of what is in heaven,' Hebrews 8:5. Christ ministers in 'the sanctuary and true tabernacle set up by the Lord, not by man,' Hebrews 8:2. The tabernacle was the shadow; He is the substance.

These links are made by the New Testament itself. The acacia wood, the rings and the number of cups on the lampstand are not given Christological meanings in Scripture, and it is wiser to let the text's own connections carry the weight.
study.god:
The first thing this chapter shows about God is His desire. Before a single measurement is given, God states His purpose: 'that I may dwell among them,' verse 8. The Creator of heaven and earth, whom 'even heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain,' 1 Kings 8:27, chooses to pitch a tent in a camp of former slaves. His transcendence is not threatened by His nearness; it is displayed in it.

He is a God who speaks rather than a God who is seen. The ark carries no image. Between the cherubim there is empty space, and from there God says, 'I will meet with you... I will speak with you,' verse 22. Deuteronomy 4:12 makes the point from Sinai: Israel 'saw no form; there was only a voice.' The centre of Israel's worship is the covenant word inside the ark and the living voice above it.

He is a God whose throne rests on His law and whose law is covered by mercy. The tablets lie beneath the mercy seat, and God's presence rests above both. Justice is not set aside, yet it is not the last word. The same arrangement that places God's commands at the heart of the sanctuary places atonement over them.

He is a God who provides and sustains. The table with its bread before His face, and the lampstand whose light never goes out, show a household that is always supplied. God does not need bread or light. These furnishings picture what He gives: food for His people, and light in the darkness. 'With You is the fountain of life; in Your light we see light,' Psalm 36:9.

He is a God of beauty. Pure gold, hammered almond blossoms and fine materials show that holiness and beauty belong together. The psalmist longs 'to gaze on the beauty of the LORD,' Psalm 27:4, and this chapter explains why the place of His presence was beautiful.

He is also a God who receives. He invites an offering from willing hearts, verse 2, not because He lacks anything but because He delights to let His people share in making room for Him.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to come to God where He has chosen to meet us, to bring our gifts gladly, and to rejoice that the God who once met Moses above the mercy seat now meets His people in Christ.

crossReferences.note: God explains the goal of the whole Exodus: He is the LORD 'who brought them out of the land of Egypt so that I might dwell among them.' Exodus 25:8 is the first step toward that goal. Redemption from slavery was always meant to lead to God's presence among His people.

When the offering of Exodus 25:2 is actually collected, the people bring so much that Moses has to stop them. The willing heart God asked for is shown in action, and it stands in stark contrast to the gold given for the calf in Exodus 32:2-4.

On the Day of Atonement the high priest sprinkles the blood of the bull and the goat on and before the mercy seat. This is where the mercy seat of Exodus 25:17 gets its meaning as the place of atonement, above the tablets of the law.

Moses enters the Tent of Meeting and hears the voice 'from between the two cherubim above the mercy seat.' The promise of Exodus 25:22, 'I will speak with you,' is fulfilled exactly as given. God's presence at the ark is a speaking presence.

Gives the regulations for the Bread of the Presence: twelve loaves in two rows, renewed every Sabbath, with frankincense as a memorial, 'as a permanent covenant.' The twelve loaves represent the twelve tribes kept continually before the LORD's face.

Jeremiah sees an almond branch, and God says He is watching over His word to fulfil it. The Hebrew for almond and for watching sound alike. The almond cups on the lampstand of Exodus 25:33 may carry a hint of this watchful God, whose light never goes out.

Paul says God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice, using the Greek word that translates 'mercy seat' in Hebrews 9:5. Christ is the place where God deals with sin and meets with sinners, displayed publicly rather than hidden behind a veil.

Jesus calls Himself the bread of life and the living bread from heaven. The Bread of the Presence lay before God to picture a people sustained in His presence; Christ gives Himself as bread 'for the life of the world,' so that whoever eats will live forever.

John turns and sees seven golden lampstands, and among them 'One like the Son of Man.' The lampstand of Exodus 25:31 becomes the picture of Christ's churches, and the risen Christ walks among them as the priest who tends the lamps.

Quotes Exodus 25:40, 'See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain,' to show that the tabernacle was 'a copy and shadow of what is in heaven.' The earthly sanctuary pointed beyond itself to Christ's ministry.

When God's temple in heaven is opened, 'the ark of His covenant appeared in His temple,' with lightning and thunder like Sinai. The ark that disappeared from Israel's history is shown to have its true counterpart in heaven, the throne of the covenant God.

The new Jerusalem has no temple, because God and the Lamb are its temple, and no need of sun or moon, because 'the Lamb is its lamp.' The dwelling and the lampstand of Exodus 25 give way to the direct presence of God and Christ.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible begins with God dwelling with humanity in a garden, and it ends with God dwelling with humanity in a city. Exodus 25 is the moment when, after the loss of Eden, God first gives His people a place for His presence to live among them. Many readers notice the echoes of the garden: gold, onyx and precious stones, Genesis 2:11-12, cherubim who once guarded the way in, Genesis 3:24, and a lampstand shaped like a flowering tree. The tabernacle is a way back toward what was lost.

It answers the question raised at the burning bush and at the Red Sea: what is all this rescue for? The song of Exodus 15:17 had already looked ahead to 'the place, O LORD, You have prepared for Your dwelling.' Chapter 25 begins to build it.

It also sets up the rest of Israel's history. The ark goes before the people into the land, sits at Shiloh, is captured and returned, and rests at last under Solomon's cherubim. The bread and the lamp are tended through the generations. Yet the tabernacle and temple remain copies. When Israel treats the ark as a charm or forgets the God it represents, the presence departs and the temple falls.

The prophets look past the furnishings. Jeremiah foresees a day when no one will miss the ark, Jeremiah 3:16. Ezekiel hears God promise, 'My dwelling place will be with them,' Ezekiel 37:27.

The story turns in Christ. The Word pitches His tent among us, John 1:14. He is the mercy seat, the bread and the light. Through Him the church becomes 'a dwelling place for God in His Spirit,' Ephesians 2:22, and the lampstands now stand for His people.

In the new creation the furnishings are no longer needed because what they pictured is fully present. There is no temple, for God and the Lamb are the temple. There is no lamp, for the Lamb is its lamp. The tree of life stands by the river, Revelation 22:2, and 'the dwelling place of God is with man,' Revelation 21:3. What Exodus 25 began in gold and acacia wood, God finishes in a new heaven and a new earth.

quiz.q: What kind of offering did God ask Moses to receive from the Israelites?

options.text: One from every man whose heart compelled him, a freewill offering.
options.note: Verse 2 specifies the offering came from those whose hearts were moved, not by compulsion.

options.text: A mandatory tax collected from every household equally.
options.note: The text specifies willing hearts, not a fixed, mandatory tax.

options.text: An offering taken only from the tribe of Levi.
options.note: The offering was requested from the whole community of Israel, not one tribe alone.

options.text: No offering was requested at all.
options.note: Verse 2 explicitly calls for an offering from willing hearts.

quiz.q: Why did God want Israel to build Him a sanctuary, according to verse 8?

options.text: So that He may dwell among them.
options.note: This is the stated purpose given directly in verse 8.

options.text: So that Israel would have a tourist attraction for other nations.
options.note: No such reason is given; the stated purpose is God's dwelling presence among His people.

options.text: Purely as a display of Israel's wealth.
options.note: The offering's purpose was worship and God's dwelling, not a display of wealth.

options.text: No reason is given for building the sanctuary.
options.note: Verse 8 explicitly states the reason: so that I may dwell among them.

quiz.q: Where did God say He would meet with Moses?

options.text: Above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim over the ark of the Testimony.
options.note: Verse 22 states this precisely as the meeting place.

options.text: At the entrance to the courtyard only.
options.note: This meeting is specifically located above the mercy seat inside the ark's covering, not merely at the courtyard entrance.

options.text: Anywhere Moses chose to pray.
options.note: God specifies one exact location, not any place of Moses' choosing.

options.text: The text gives no specific meeting place.
options.note: Verse 22 explicitly names the mercy seat between the cherubim as the meeting place.

quiz.q: What was to be placed on the table at all times, according to verse 30?

options.text: The Bread of the Presence.
options.note: Verse 30 commands this bread be kept before the LORD continually.

options.text: A bowl of incense.
options.note: Incense was burned on a separate altar; the table specifically held the Bread of the Presence.

options.text: The tablets of the Testimony.
options.note: The tablets were placed inside the ark, not on the table.

options.text: Nothing was placed on the table.
options.note: Verse 30 explicitly commands the Bread of the Presence be kept there at all times.

quiz.q: How many lamps were set on the golden lampstand?

options.text: Seven.
options.note: Verse 37 specifies seven lamps set up to illuminate the area in front of the lampstand.

options.text: Twelve, one for each tribe.
options.note: Twelve is the number of tribes and of the memorial stones, not the number of lamps here.

options.text: Three.
options.note: Three cups of almond blossoms appear on each branch, but the number of lamps is seven.

options.text: The number of lamps is not specified.
options.note: Verse 37 explicitly specifies seven lamps.

questions: God asked for an offering only from those whose hearts were willing, not by compulsion. What would it look like to give to God's work this week out of genuine willingness rather than obligation?

God's purpose for the sanctuary was 'so that I may dwell among them.' How does it change your view of worship to remember that its ultimate goal is God's presence with His people, not merely rituals performed correctly?
Moses was shown an exact pattern and told to follow it precisely, not improvise. Where might you be tempted to approach God on your own terms rather than the terms He has revealed in Christ?

The mercy seat was the place where covenant law and God's meeting with His people came together. How does knowing that Christ is your true mercy seat change how you deal with your own failures to keep God's law?
The Bread of the Presence and the golden lampstand pictured ongoing provision and light in God's presence. Where in your life this week do you most need to trust Christ as your bread and light?

translationNotes.note: According to the pattern I show you, tavnit, likely indicates Moses received either a vision or a detailed model of the tabernacle's heavenly counterpart, a point Hebrews 8:5 draws on directly.
Mercy seat translates kapporet, related to the Hebrew root for atonement or covering; some translations render it 'atonement cover,' emphasizing its function on the Day of Atonement in Leviticus 16.

Bread of the Presence, literally 'bread of the face,' refers to twelve loaves kept continually before the LORD, later eaten by the priests, Leviticus 24:5-9, symbolizing Israel's ongoing communion with God.
